title: Cap. X Arg. X / Corvinus: Contra Tilen. p.148 — not ‘God does not give, therefore he never willed to give,’ but ‘he wills gifts only to the little and obedient’
latin: Nullius momenti est quod huic argumento respondetur a Corvino, Contra Tilen. pag. 148. Non sequitur, inquit, Deus huic non dat fidem aut perseverantiam aut salutem, Ergo non voluit ei dare fidem, perseverantiam aut salutem: sed hoc potius; Deus non vult dare praedicta dona nisi parvulis, laborantibus et voluntatem Patris facientibus. Ergo huic data haec dona non fuerunt, quia talis non fuit, culpa scilicet sua.
pass_a: Of no moment is that which is answered unto this argument by Corvinus, Contra Tilen. pag. 148. It does not follow, he says, God does not give unto this man faith or perseverance or salvation, Therefore he did not will to give unto him faith, perseverance or salvation: but rather this; God does not will to give the foresaid gifts except unto little ones, unto those who labour and do the Father’s will. Therefore unto this man these gifts were not given, because he was not such, namely by his own fault.
pass_b: Corvinus’s reply (Contra Tilenum, p. 148) is of no weight. It does not follow, he says, that because God does not give this man faith, perseverance, or salvation, therefore he never willed to give them—but rather this: God wills those gifts only to the little, to those who labor and do the Father’s will. So this man did not receive them because he was not such—namely by his own fault.

title: Cap. X Arg. X reply: question is predestinating will to do or not do — God gave Peter faith eternally willed; not giving Judas proves preterition/reprobation
latin: Respondeo, Corvinum immemorem plane esse qua de re disputetur. Non enim quaestio est de voluntate Dei sub qualibet notione, sed de voluntate Dei praedestinantis aliquid facere aut non facere. Est autem optima et firmissima consequentia; Deus dedit fidem, perseverantiam, et vitam aeternam Petro, Ergo voluntate praedestinante ab aeterno voluit illi dare fidem, perseverantiam et vitam aeternam. Et e contra non minus firma est illa: Deus non dedit Judae fidem, perseverantiam et vitam aeternam: Ergo illum praeteriit, non praedestinavit, reprobavit, tantis bonis afficere noluit.
pass_a: I answer that Corvinus is plainly forgetful of the matter under dispute. For the question is not of God’s will under any notion whatever, but of the will of God predestinating to do something or not to do it. And it is the best and firmest consequence; God gave faith, perseverance, and everlasting life unto Peter, Therefore by a predestinating will from eternity he willed to give him faith, perseverance and everlasting life. And on the contrary that is no less firm: God did not give unto Judas faith, perseverance and everlasting life: Therefore he passed him by, did not predestinate him, reprobated him, was unwilling to affect him with such great goods.
pass_b: I answer: Corvinus has plainly forgotten what is under dispute. The question is not God’s will under any notion, but God’s will as predestinating to do or not do. This consequence is best and firmest: God gave Peter faith, perseverance, and everlasting life; therefore by predestinating will from eternity he willed to give him those goods. No less firm the reverse: God did not give Judas faith, perseverance, and everlasting life; therefore he passed him by, did not predestine him, reprobated him, and would not affect him with such great goods.

title: Cap. X Arg. X: Corvinus’s ‘only to the little and obedient’ fails — same question returns; if God willed humility for Judas as for Peter, both would have it
latin: Quod autem subjungit Corvinus, id solum sequi, Deum non velle dare praedicta bona nisi parvulis et obedientibus, atque idcirco non fuisse data Judae, quia sua culpa talis non fuit; primo non valet; quia eadem quaestio adhuc manet de hac parvitate et obedientia, quae mota fuit de fide et salute. Quaero enim cur Deus non dederit hanc parvitatem et obedientiam Judae quam dedit Petro. Si voluisset pariter dare utrique, in utroque pariter exstitisset. Nam Deo volenti bonam humilitatis aut parvitatis qualitatem indere humanae voluntati, nullum resistit hominis arbitrium: Tali equidem voluntati non resistitur, quia velle non resistere in ipso homine operatur: Non enim ultra resistit voluntas cui velle resistere sublatum est.
pass_a: But what Corvinus subjoins, that this alone follows, that God does not will to give the foresaid goods except unto little ones and the obedient, and therefore they were not given unto Judas, because by his own fault he was not such; first it does not hold; because the same question still remains concerning this littleness and obedience which was moved concerning faith and salvation. For I ask why God did not give unto Judas this littleness and obedience which he gave unto Peter. If he had willed to give alike unto both, it would have alike existed in both. For unto God willing to put into the human will the good quality of humility or littleness, no man’s free will resists: Unto such a will indeed there is no resisting, because to will not to resist is wrought in the man himself: For the will resists no further when the willing to resist has been taken away.
pass_b: What Corvinus adds—that it only follows God wills those goods to the little and obedient, so Judas lacked them by his own fault—fails first: the same question returns about that littleness and obedience that was asked about faith and salvation. Why did God not give Judas the littleness and obedience he gave Peter? Had he willed to give alike to both, it would have stood alike in both. When God wills to plant humility or littleness in the human will, no free will resists—such a will is not resisted, because willing not to resist is worked in the man himself; the will resists no further once willing to resist is taken away.

lemmas.gloss: God’s will to give humility is unresisted

title: Cap. X Arg. X: suspending gifts on prior littleness is Pelagian unless littleness itself is God’s special gift — Orange canon 6; preparing littleness for one is electing
latin: Dein, qui haec dona Dei suspendunt ex parvitate praeeunte, nisi fateantur hanc ipsam parvitatem esse speciale donum Dei, in Pelagianismum incidunt, et incurrunt in Canonem 6. Concilii Arausicani: Si autem fateantur, perinde est concedere Deum praeparasse et donasse hanc parvitatem, unde fides et salus dependet, uni et non alteri, atque praeparasse et donasse ipsam fidem et salutem; quod nihil aliud est, quam unum elegisse, alterum reprobasse.
pass_a: Next, those who suspend these gifts of God from preceding littleness, unless they confess that this very littleness is a special gift of God, fall into Pelagianism, and run upon Canon 6 of the Council of Orange: But if they confess it, it is all one to grant that God prepared and gave this littleness, whence faith and salvation hang, unto one and not unto the other, and prepared and gave faith itself and salvation; which is nothing other than to have elected one, to have reprobated the other.
pass_b: Next: those who hang these gifts on prior littleness, unless they admit that littleness itself is God’s special gift, fall into Pelagianism and hit Orange canon 6. If they do admit it, that is the same as granting God prepared and gave that littleness—on which faith and salvation hang—to one and not the other, and prepared and gave faith and salvation themselves; which is nothing other than electing one and reprobating the other.

title: Cap. X Arg. X close: reprobates lack saving grace because they are not what God requires — that itself proves antecedent rejection; Col. i. 12; no middle between election and reprobation
latin: Denique, quod dicit Corvinus, reprobis non dari gratiam salutiferam, quia sua culpa tales non sunt, quales Deus praerequirit, hoc ipsum arguit eos fuisse antecedenter rejectos sive praeteritos: Nam Deus decrevit omnes electos tales efficere, quales ad capessendum gratiam et gloriam ipse solet praerequirere, Coloss. i. 12. Quos ergo tales non effecit, eos non elegit; et quia non datur medium inter electionem et reprobationem, eosdem reprobavit. Post tot anfractus et gyros huc itaque redeamus oportet, ut quibus gratia fidei, poenitentiae et perseverantiae data non fuerit, eos in ordinatione ad vitam aeternam praeteritos agnoscamus; sicut e contra, eos quibus haec fuerunt praeparata et donata, electos confiteamur. Atque ut quidam electi fuerunt misericorditer ad haec bona ante praevisionem eorundem ut in illis existentium, ita quidam praeteriti fuerunt, et ad talia accipienda haud praedestinati, antequam praeviderentur ut talibus bonis finaliter carentes.
pass_a: Finally, what Corvinus says, that saving grace is not given unto the reprobate because by their own fault they are not such as God prerequires, this itself argues that they were antecedently rejected or passed by: For God has decreed to make all the elect such as he himself is wont to prerequire unto taking hold of grace and glory, Coloss. i. 12. Those therefore whom he has not made such, them he has not elected; and because no middle is given between election and reprobation, the same he has reprobated. After so many windings and turns we must therefore return hither, that those unto whom the grace of faith, repentance and perseverance has not been given, we acknowledge as passed by in the ordination unto everlasting life; just as on the contrary we confess as elect those unto whom these things have been prepared and given. And as certain ones were mercifully elected unto these goods before foresight of the same as existing in them, so certain ones were passed by, and by no means predestinated unto receiving such things, before they were foreseen as finally lacking such goods.
pass_b: Finally Corvinus says saving grace is not given to the reprobate because by their fault they are not what God prerequires—and that itself proves they were antecedently rejected or passed by. For God has decreed to make all the elect such as he is wont to prerequire for laying hold of grace and glory (Col. i. 12). Those he has not made such, he has not elected; and since there is no middle between election and reprobation, he has reprobated them. After so many twists we must come back here: those not given the grace of faith, repentance, and perseverance we acknowledge as passed by in the ordination to everlasting life; those for whom these were prepared and given we confess as elect. And as some were mercifully elected to these goods before foresight of them as existing in them, so some were passed by and not predestined to receive such things before they were foreseen as finally lacking them.

lemmas.gloss: lack of required qualities proves prior rejection

lemmas.lemma: non datur medium inter electionem et reprobationem

title: Cap. X Ultimum open: absolute predestination/preterition from mere divine good pleasure is not Augustine’s private opinion but received by anti-Pelagian councils — against Arminius/Corvinus
latin: Ultimum nostrum argumentum jam proponemus, in quo conabimur ostendere hanc sententiam de praedestinatione quorundam, et praeteritione aliorum ex mero voluntatis Divinae beneplacito, absque omni praecedaneo respectu ad oppositos hominum actus, sive bonos sive malos, non fuisse singularem quandam Augustini aut discipulorum ejus opinionem, sed receptam et probatam ab illis Conciliis quae contra Pelagium et Semipelagianos fuerunt celebrata. Hoc idcirco faciendum putavimus, quia Arminius, Corvinus, reliquique novatores confidenter asserunt, doctrinam hanc nostram in nullo Concilio fuisse approbatam, ne quidem in iis quae contra Pelagium fuere habita. Huic tamen argumento quaedam sunt a nobis necessario praemittenda.
pass_a: We will now propose our last argument, in which we shall endeavour to show that this sentence concerning the predestination of certain ones, and the preterition of others from the mere good pleasure of the Divine will, without any preceding respect unto opposite acts of men, whether good or evil, was not some singular opinion of Augustine or of his disciples, but received and approved by those Councils which were celebrated against Pelagius and the Semipelagians. This we have thought fit to do for this reason, because Arminius, Corvinus, and the rest of the innovators confidently assert that this our doctrine was approved in no Council, not even in those which were held against Pelagius. Yet unto this argument certain things must of necessity be premised by us.
pass_b: We now propose our last argument: to show that this teaching—the predestination of some and preterition of others from the mere good pleasure of the divine will, with no prior regard to opposite human acts, good or evil—was not some private opinion of Augustine or his disciples, but received and approved by the councils held against Pelagius and the Semipelagians. We do this because Arminius, Corvinus, and the other innovators boldly claim our doctrine was approved in no council—not even those against Pelagius. Yet certain premises must first be laid down.

lemmas.gloss: last argument: councils receive absolute view

title: Cap. X Ultimum Prima: early anti-Pelagian councils did not expressly define absolute predestination — yet defined much that cannot stand if absolute gratuitous predestination is overturned; Faustus condemned
latin: Primo, fatemur, Concilia quae celebrata fuerunt contra Pelagium et Semipelagianos ipsius Augustini temporibus, aut saeculo ab obitu ejus proximo, qualia fuerunt Diospolitanum, Milevitanum, Carthaginense, Arausicanum, aliaque nonnulla, non expresse, directe et particulariter sanxisse doctrinam de absoluta praedestinatione, aut condemnasse opinionem contrariam de electione et reprobatione ex praevisione diversorum actuum in hominibus. Illud tamen affirmamus, in hisce Conciliis multa fuisse definita quae stare non possunt absoluta et gratuita praedestinatione eversa, aut posita illa conditionata electione et praeteritione quam Faustus, et post illum alii nonnulli, ac tandem Arminius excolendam et defendendam susceperunt. Huc accedit, Fausti libros in quibus conditionatam illam electionem operose stabilire conatur, et absolutam explodere, damnatos fuisse ab antiqua Ecclesia, ut ex Gratiano liquet, Distinct. 15. Decretum extat a Tom. Conciliorum, et sancitum fuit a Gelasio in Synodo septuaginta Episcoporum. Hormisda etiam de Fausti libro consultus respondet, Doctrinam Catholicam ex Augustino et Prospero, non item e Fausto, disci oportere.
pass_a: First, we confess that the Councils which were celebrated against Pelagius and the Semipelagians in Augustine’s own times, or in the age next after his death—such as were Diospolis, Milevis, Carthage, Orange, and some others—did not expressly, directly and particularly sanction the doctrine of absolute predestination, or condemn the contrary opinion of election and reprobation from foresight of diverse acts in men. Yet this we affirm, that in these Councils many things were defined which cannot stand if absolute and gratuitous predestination be overturned, or if that conditioned election and preterition be laid down which Faustus, and after him some others, and at length Arminius undertook to cultivate and defend. Hither also it comes that Faustus’s books, in which he laboriously tries to establish that conditioned election and to explode the absolute, were condemned by the ancient Church, as is clear from Gratian, Distinct. 15. The Decree stands in the Tom. of Councils, and was sanctioned by Gelasius in a Synod of seventy Bishops. Hormisdas also, consulted concerning Faustus’s book, answers that Catholic doctrine ought to be learned from Augustine and Prosper, not likewise from Faustus.
pass_b: First we confess: the councils against Pelagius and the Semipelagians in Augustine’s time or the age just after his death—Diospolis, Milevis, Carthage, Orange, and others—did not expressly, directly, and particularly sanction absolute predestination or condemn foresight-election and reprobation. Yet we affirm that much defined in those councils cannot stand if absolute gratuitous predestination is overturned, or if that conditioned election and preterition is set up which Faustus, then others, and at last Arminius undertook to cultivate and defend. Add that Faustus’s books, which labor to fix conditioned election and explode the absolute, were condemned by the ancient church—clear from Gratian, Distinctio 15; the decree stands in the councils’ Tomus, sanctioned by Gelasius in a synod of seventy bishops. Hormisdas, asked about Faustus’s book, answers that catholic doctrine should be learned from Augustine and Prosper, not from Faustus.

title: Cap. X Ultimum Secunda open: Orthodox predestination must be gathered from what they settled on Grace — Augustine: predestination is grace’s preparation; Vasquez: same question of grace and predestination
latin: Atque inter caetera vel praecipue spectasse doctrinam hanc de conditionata praedestinatione, inde probabile est: quod Petrus Diaconus, aliique orthodoxi ex Oriente Romam missi, hoc nomine potissimum Fausti libros anathematizandos censuerunt, quod contra praedestinationis sententiam scripti essent, De incarn. et grat. cap. ultimo. Secundo dicimus, Nos et posse et debere colligere quae fuerit Orthodoxorum de praedestinatione sententia ex illis quae de Gratia contra Pelagianos et Pelagianorum reliquias statuerunt. Nam ut inquit Augustinus, De praedest. sanctor. cap. 10, inter gratiam et praedestinationem hoc tantum interest, quod praedestinatio sit gratiae praeparatio, gratia vero ipsa donatio. Si quis igitur doceat gratiam Christi salutiferam ex absoluta Dei voluntate dependere, et minime dari hominibus aut negari pro diversis illorum operationibus, is de praedestinatione et praeteritione, si sibi constare velit, idem statuat est necesse.
pass_a: And among other things that this doctrine of conditioned predestination was chiefly looked to is probable from this: that Peter the Deacon and other orthodox men sent from the East unto Rome judged Faustus’s books chiefly for this cause to be anathematized, because they had been written against the sentence of predestination, De incarn. et grat. cap. last. Secondly we say that We both can and ought to gather what was the Orthodox sentence concerning predestination from those things which they established concerning Grace against the Pelagians and the remnants of the Pelagians. For as Augustine says, De praedest. sanctor. cap. 10, between grace and predestination this alone differs, that predestination is the preparation of grace, but grace itself the gift. If therefore anyone teach that Christ’s saving grace hangs from the absolute will of God, and is by no means given unto men or denied according to their diverse operations, he must of necessity, if he will be consistent with himself, establish the same concerning predestination and preterition.
pass_b: That conditioned predestination was chiefly in view is likely from this: Peter the Deacon and other eastern orthodox sent to Rome judged Faustus’s books especially to be anathematized because they were written against the sentence of predestination (De incarnatione et gratia, last chapter). Second: we can and must gather the Orthodox view of predestination from what they settled on Grace against the Pelagians and their remnants. For as Augustine says (De praedestinatione sanctorum 10), between grace and predestination this alone differs: predestination is grace’s preparation; grace itself is the gift. So anyone who teaches that Christ’s saving grace hangs on God’s absolute will, and is not given or denied according to men’s diverse operations, must—if he would be consistent—hold the same of predestination and preterition.
